newsitem.title: USA: U.S. lacks tools to fight computer attack - expert.
newsitem.headline: U.S. lacks tools to fight computer attack - expert.

text.p: The United States lacks the tools to fight a possible computer assault on critical infrastructure such as telecommunications, banking and power grids, the head of a White House panel said on Wednesday.
No such attack is imminent, but is sure to present itself eventually, Robert Marsh, head of the President's Commission on Critical Infrastructure Protection, told reporters.

"We couldn't find the 'smoking keyboard'; there isn't a country out there with a war plan ... but it's sure to evolve," Marsh said. "There isn't a firewall (to protect computer systems) that a group of experts can't get around."

Key areas of infrastructure vulnerable to "cyber" threats are telecommunications, electric power systems -- including system control and data acquisition -- and banking and finance, according to Marsh.
The banking community "will not deny" it is losing billions of dollars to cyber-criminals, and accepts this as a cost of doing business, Marsh said.
"We don't have the tools to identify what's going on," Marsh said. "We're at a very primitive phase of understanding threats to these infrastructures."

Part of the problem is a reluctance both by U.S. government agencies and by private industry to reveal cyber-weaknesses. Another hurdle is the global nature of business and computer networks, wherein a U.S.-based component might cooperate but a foreign-based one might balk.

The unsecured nature of the Internet presents other difficulties, not least of which is the free flow of information which could give a disgruntled hacker enough data to bring down a critical system, Marsh said.
So far most incursions into government systems have been by "recreational" hackers who simply want to show they have gained access, he said.

The commission is also charged with assessing the possible physical threat to property, but that is less of a research challenge, according to Marsh. In addition to cyber-systems, the panel is looking at other vital infrastructure including gas and oil systems, transportation and water supply.
The commission aims to find where infrastructure is vulnerable and develop a strategy to make it more secure. Established last July, the panel's final report on subject is expected by October.
